identification.bodyShape: Elongated, laterally compressed mackerel body, fully scaled except for the pectoral fins.
identificationTraits: Lateral line dips sharply downward below the second dorsal fin, then runs wavy toward the tail — the clearest field mark separating it from Spanish mackerel, whose lateral line curves gently.
First (spiny) dorsal fin is gray/colorless with no black blotch, unlike the black-tipped first dorsal fin of Spanish mackerel.
No prominent golden-yellow spots on the sides as adults, unlike Spanish mackerel's golden spotting.
Two dorsal fins separated by a gap; the first retracts into a groove in the body.
7–10 finlets follow the second dorsal and anal fins.
Large mouth with roughly 30 large, closely spaced, triangular, uniform teeth per jaw side.
identification.coloration: Iron-gray to olive back fading gradually to silvery sides and belly with an iridescent sheen; juveniles show faint yellow markings that disappear with maturity.
identification.juvenileAppearance: Young fish show lateral yellow markings that fade as the fish matures.
identification.adultAppearance: Iron-gray back and silvery sides, no black blotch on the first dorsal fin, and no bold golden spotting; the sharply dipping lateral line is the most reliable field mark against Spanish mackerel.

similarSpecies.name: Spanish mackerel
similarSpecies.distinction: Spanish mackerel is smaller, shows a gently curved lateral line (versus king mackerel's sharp dip), a black blotch on the front of the first dorsal fin, and prominent golden-yellow spots along the sides — all absent in king mackerel.

identification.averageAdultLength: A sourced population-average length was not found; see commonAnglingSize and maximumDocumentedSize.
identification.commonAnglingSize: Legal recreational fish start around 24 in fork length in South Atlantic states; many landed fish run well under the maximum size.
identification.typicalWeight: A sourced population-average weight was not found; fish over about 30 lb are commonly regarded as large ('smoker' kings).
identification.maximumDocumentedSize: Up to about 5.5 ft and 100 lb.
identification.longevity: Documented to more than 20 years; sexual maturity reached around age 2.

social.note: Adults typically travel and feed in schools.

feedingStrategy.note: Voracious pursuit predator on schooling baitfish (menhaden, jacks, cutlassfish, and similar), plus crustaceans and, rarely, mollusks; documented leaping clear of the water in pursuit of prey. Adults favor prey roughly 10–15 cm long.

dielTendency.note: Not clearly sourced by time of day; classified as mixed pending a source-backed determination rather than left blank, since the field is required.

behavior.depthMovement: Ranges to the edge of the continental shelf (about 200 m) but is most common under about 80 m; moves onto the inner shelf and closer inshore in summer and around higher tides.
behavior.thermalDrivenBehavior: Migration is strongly temperature-driven: fish winter in a mixing zone off south Florida and move north (Atlantic group) or toward the northern Gulf and Mexico (Gulf group) in spring and summer as water warms, reversing in fall. Field-reported range runs roughly 20–31°C for larvae, with a roughly 20°C (about 68°F) threshold below which adults are seldom found, reported independently by two agency-adjacent sources.
behavior.coverUse: Not strongly structure-dependent; associates more with bait concentrations, temperature breaks, and current edges than with hard structure, though it uses nearshore reefs and wrecks where bait holds.
behavior.openWaterBehavior: A coastal pelagic species that ranges widely in open water tracking bait schools and temperature structure rather than holding to one location.
behavior.seasonalActivity: Strong seasonal migrator, moving north and inshore in spring–summer and south and offshore in fall–winter, converging in a shared winter zone off south Florida.
behavior.spawningBehavior: Batch spawner over an extended spring-through-fall window on the outer continental shelf; this record excludes specific spawning locations as conservation context only.

diet.primaryNote: Voracious pursuit predator on schooling baitfish (menhaden, jacks, cutlassfish, and similar), with crustaceans and, rarely, mollusks also taken; adults favor prey around 10–15 cm. Diet capacity is not evidence of a current bait event.

lifeStageDiet.adult: Schooling baitfish predominate, with crustaceans and occasional mollusks also taken.

diet.preySizeShifts: Adults favor prey fish roughly 10–15 cm long; a full ontogenetic prey-size progression from juvenile to adult was not found in an acceptable source.
diet.observedForageRule: Diet capacity described here is not proof of a current feeding event; what king mackerel are actually eating on a given day still has to come from direct observation.

seasonal_calendar.overview: King mackerel is a strongly migratory coastal pelagic that follows temperature and bait: moving inshore and north or west as water warms in spring and summer, then concentrating south toward a shared winter zone off south Florida as it cools. Presentation classes here reflect its bait-school and current-structure association, not a location or timing recommendation.

entries.habitatClass: Nearshore and offshore water, moving onto the inner shelf and closer inshore as water warms and on higher tides.
entries.movementTendency: Beginning of the northward and inshore seasonal migration.
entries.thermalContext: Movement tracks the roughly 20°C / 68°F threshold reported for the species.
entries.presentationImplication: Live-bait slow troll and trolling near bait concentrations nearshore; tide-line drift along temperature breaks and current rips offshore.
entries.conservationNote: Spawning begins in this window on the outer shelf in part of the range; specific locations are excluded from this record.

entries.habitatClass: Continues an inshore/nearshore presence associated with bait schools and temperature breaks; the migratory group's northern range extent reaches its seasonal peak.
entries.presentationImplication: Live-bait slow troll and tide-line drift nearshore; trolling spread along offshore temperature breaks and weed lines.
entries.conservationNote: Spawning continues through this season per sourced material.

entries.habitatClass: Begins moving south and offshore as water cools.
entries.movementTendency: Southward migration toward the shared winter zone.
entries.presentationImplication: Trolling spread and tide-line drift along temperature breaks and current edges offshore; live-bait slow troll nearshore.

entries.habitatClass: Concentrated in the shared winter mixing zone off south Florida for much of the migratory population.
entries.presentationImplication: Live-bait slow troll and other structure-associated nearshore techniques where bait holds; a distinct offshore presentation family was not separately sourced for this period.
